articles.title: People with excessive smartphone habits show distinct neural responses to social exclusion
articles.summary: A recent brain imaging study reveals that people with excessive smartphone habits process social exclusion differently than average users. Heightened brain activity in pain-processing regions suggests that heavy screen use is tied to a distinct sensitivity to social rejection.

articles.title: A baby girl appears to alter a father’s relationship priorities in one highly specific way
articles.summary: Does the sex of your child influence your marriage? New psychological research suggests that having a daughter prompts fathers to invest significantly more time and energy into their romantic partnership than having a son.

articles.title: Children’s math and reading skills are linked to better maternal health in midlife
articles.summary: A new analysis of longitudinal data reveals a surprising cross-generational connection: mothers whose children excel in math and reading tend to experience better physical and mental health during their middle-aged years.

articles.title: Disgust predicts conservative views most strongly in people with low bodily awareness
articles.summary: Being easily disgusted is often linked to conservative political views, but a new study reveals a surprising catch. This connection is actually strongest among individuals who are least aware of their own internal bodily sensations.

articles.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
articles.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

articles.title: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep
articles.summary: Caffeine may make sleep less restorative even when you fall asleep normally and stay in bed for eight hours, with EEG recordings revealing fewer of the slow brain waves associated with deep sleep. Individual sensitivity varies dramatically, meaning even caffeine consumed earlier in the day could affect nighttime recovery for some people.

articles.title: Rare pregnancy infections may triple the risk of autism
articles.summary: A major Swedish study of 3.7 million people has found that rare TORCH infections passed from a pregnant woman to the fetus are linked to much higher risks of autism and intellectual disability later in life. Children with a congenital TORCH infection were about three times more likely to be diagnosed with autism, more than seven times more likely to have an intellectual disability, and up to 30 times more likely to have severe to profound intellectual disability.

articles.title: Brain structure changes appear seven years before Alzheimer’s plaques are detected
articles.summary: New research indicates that changes in the brain's outer layer can be detected at least seven years before amyloid plaques reach high levels. This challenges the traditional timeline of how Alzheimer's disease develops.
